plan.concept: Scaled dot-product attention: scores QK^T/sqrt(d_k), softmax over keys, weighted sum of V.
learning_outcomes: Compute similarity scores between a query and all keys.
Explain why dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps softmax out of saturated regions.
Show that each row of attention weights sums to 1 and the output is the weighted sum of V rows.
plan.visual_strategy: Editable Q, K, V matrices feed a pipeline of scores -> scaled scores -> softmax weights -> output; heatmaps and bars show each stage; a sweep shows how scaling changes weight sharpness as d_k grows.
plan.misconception: Scaling is not a normalization of the output; it only rescales the logits before softmax, changing how peaked the weights are.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step

paper.title: Attention Is All You Need
paper.authors: Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser, Polosukhin

idea: Attention maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output. Each query is compared with every key by a dot product; after dividing by sqrt(d_k) and applying softmax, the resulting weights say how much of each value vector to mix. The output is that weighted sum of the value vectors.
why_it_matters: This single formula is the core operation of the Transformer: it lets every position gather information from all other positions in one parallel matrix multiply. The sqrt(d_k) scaling is what keeps the softmax trainable when key/query dimensions are large.

equations.caption: Softmax turns scores into weights that sum to 1.
For independent unit-variance components, dot products grow with d_k (footnote 1).

symbols.meaning: matrix of queries, one row per query position, each row of length $d_k$
matrix of keys, one row per key position, each row of length $d_k$
matrix of values, one row per key position, each row of length $d_v$
dimension of queries and keys (number of columns of Q and K)
dimension of values (number of columns of V)
raw score matrix $QK^{T}$, shape (queries x keys)
attention weight matrix after softmax, each row sums to 1
output matrix $AV$, one row per query

walkthrough: Take one query row $q$ and every key row $k_j$; compute raw scores $s_j = q\cdot k_j$ (the matrix $S=QK^{T}$).
Divide each score by $\sqrt{d_k}$ to get scaled logits $z_j = s_j/\sqrt{d_k}$.
Apply softmax over the keys: $a_j = e^{z_j}/\sum_m e^{z_m}$, giving a row of weights that sums to 1.
Form the output for that query as the weighted sum $o = \sum_j a_j v_j$; stacking rows gives $O=AV$.
Repeat for every query row; each row of $A$ is an independent probability distribution over the keys.

explorations.title: Equal scores give uniform weights
explorations.change: Set all three rows of K equal (as in the preset) and keep scaling on.
explorations.observe: Every raw score in a row is identical, so A has 1/3 in each cell and rowSums = 1 for both queries; O becomes the average of the three V rows, (0.667, 0.667).
explorations.why: Softmax of equal logits is uniform, so the output is the plain mean of the values.

explorations.title: A dominant key and the role of sqrt(d_k)
explorations.change: Give q1 a large dot product with k1 (preset), then toggle 'Divide scores by sqrt(d_k)' off.
explorations.observe: With scaling on, z1 = 27/sqrt(3) = 15.59 and the weight on k1 is about 1.0 (maxWeight ~ 1). With scaling off, z1 = 27, the softmax is even more saturated, and the output row for q1 stays essentially v1 = (1, 0).
explorations.why: Dividing by sqrt(d_k) shrinks logits so softmax keeps usable gradients; without it, large d_k pushes softmax into a near one-hot region.

misconception.title: Common misunderstanding
misconception.text: The $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor is not a normalization of the output or of the values. It only rescales the logits before softmax; the weights still sum to 1 either way, but their sharpness changes. The paper's footnote 1 shows why: for independent unit-variance components, $q\cdot k$ has variance $d_k$, so the logits grow like $\sqrt{d_k}$ unless divided by it.

checks.name: Output equals weighted sum of V

Uniform keys give uniform weights (worked example)

from_paper: Attention maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the output is a weighted sum of the values and the weight is a compatibility function of the query with the key (Section 3.2).
The input consists of queries and keys of dimension d_k and values of dimension d_v; dot products are divided by sqrt(d_k) and softmax gives the weights (Section 3.2.1).
For independent unit-variance components, the dot product has mean 0 and variance d_k, so scaling counteracts large logits (footnote 1).
our_simplifications: We use tiny editable matrices (2 queries, 3 keys, d_k = 3, d_v = 2) instead of the paper's d_k = d_v = 64 and h = 8 heads.
We add a softmax temperature T (default 1) purely as a teaching knob; the paper uses T = 1.
The sweep view varies T rather than d_k because d_k is fixed by the matrix shape in this toy.
No training, masking, positional encoding, or multi-head projection is shown.
quotes: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by $\sqrt{d_{k}}$ , and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.
To counteract this effect, we scale the dot products by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}$ .
